meta.subtitle: Honeywell spin-off in specialty materials, with accelerating sales and raised 2026 guidance set against a debt-financed Element Solutions acquisition.

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Solstice BUY with a $68–$84 target range against a $57.98 price (September 23, 2026). The stock trades at 43.9x trailing GAAP earnings, but that multiple is distorted by spin-off and transaction costs and by interest that began only after the October 30, 2025 separation from Honeywell; on consensus forward estimates the shares sit at 20.1x NTM and about 17.2x FY27E EPS of $3.37. Second-quarter net sales rose 11% to $1,148 million — roughly 7.0% volume and 3.6% price — and management raised full-year 2026 guidance to $4,125–$4,185 million of net sales and $2.75–$2.95 of adjusted diluted EPS. Growth was broad: RAS net sales rose 12% on Refrigerants (+13%), Nuclear ({+ +27% +}) and Healthcare Packaging (+24%), while ESM rose 8% led by Electronic Materials (+15%). The offsets are real. The spin loaded about $2.0B of total debt and a $1.5B FY25 dividend onto a balance sheet that carried none the year before, RAS adjusted EBITDA margin {- fell 648 basis points to 32.9% -} on turnaround timing, and the pending acquisition of Element Solutions — $10.00 cash plus 0.500 Solstice shares per share, backed by a $4.685 billion bridge — adds integration and leverage risk before it closes in the first half of 2027. With less than a year of standalone results since the spin-off, the range of outcomes is wide; the BUY rests on continued double-digit organic growth and a partial re-rating toward the Street's $80.25 consensus target, tempered by a genuine bear case.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Solstice Advanced Materials is a specialty chemicals and advanced materials company headquartered in Morris Plains, New Jersey, incorporated in 2025 and spun off from Honeywell on October 30, 2025, when Honeywell shareowners received one Solstice share for every four Honeywell shares. It now trades on Nasdaq under the ticker SOLS. The company operates two segments. Refrigerants & Applied Solutions (RAS) makes low global warming potential refrigerants, blowing agents, solvents and aerosol materials and provides conversion services for the nuclear energy sector, sold under the Solstice, Genetron and Aclar brands into HVAC/R, automotive, nuclear energy, insulation and healthcare markets. Electronic & Specialty Materials (ESM) supplies electronic materials, high-strength fibers and laboratory life science chemicals, including sputtering targets and high-purity solutions under the Spectra, Fluka and Hydranal brands, into semiconductor, defense, pharmaceutical and construction markets. Solstice serves over 3,000 customers in approximately 120 countries and territories from 20 manufacturing sites and four standalone research and development sites as of June 30, 2026, supported by a portfolio of over 5,700 patents and pending applications and approximately 4,100 employees.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: The investment case is a re-rating story on improving standalone execution. After years of low-single-digit growth under Honeywell (FY24 +3.3%, FY25 +3.1%), sales are accelerating: Q2'26 net sales rose 11% to $1,148 million on 7.0% volume and 3.6% price, and management raised 2026 guidance for both revenue and adjusted EPS. On consensus forward estimates the shares trade at 20.1x NTM and about 17.2x FY27E EPS of $3.37, below where the Street's $80.25 consensus target implies they should. The counter-case is that reported GAAP earnings are thin: the stock trades at 43.9x trailing-twelve-month GAAP earnings, and FY25 diluted EPS was only $1.49, down from $3.74 in FY24, both weighed by roughly $2.0B of new spin debt and a step-up in interest expense; the pending Element Solutions acquisition then layers a $4.685 billion bridge and integration risk on top before it closes in the first half of 2027. The stock is a BUY if organic momentum holds and the deal is digested; it is not if leverage or a cyclical slowdown compresses the multiple.

catalysts: Element Solutions acquisition: the $10.00-cash-plus-0.500-share deal, expected to close in the first half of 2027, would scale the platform, and its financing and integration terms are the dominant swing factor for the equity.
Continued double-digit organic growth: management guided third-quarter net sales to $990–$1,030 million, and holding that pace would extend the run.
Further guidance raises: management lifted full-year 2026 net sales to $4,125–$4,185 million and adjusted diluted EPS to $2.75–$2.95, and additional raises would support the re-rating.
Growth concentrated in the higher-margin RAS segment: Nuclear net sales rose 27% and Healthcare Packaging 24% in Q2'26, the lines best placed to support the blended margin.
risks: Leverage and deal financing: the spin loaded new debt onto a previously debt-free balance sheet, and the Element Solutions acquisition must be refinanced out of its bridge facility before closing.
Depressed GAAP earnings: the trailing multiple looks rich because spin and interest costs have compressed reported EPS, so the case leans on adjusted and forward numbers holding up.
Margin pressure: RAS adjusted EBITDA margin fell 648 basis points to 32.9% in Q2'26 on plant-turnaround timing, and group gross margin has slipped from 35.2% in FY23 to 32.2% in FY25.

Limited standalone history: Solstice has less than a year of results as an independent public company since the October 30, 2025 spin-off, and its Honeywell-era financials may not predict future results.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter net sales rose 11% to $1,148 million from $1,033 million, with the MD&A attributing 7.0% to volume, 3.6% to price and 0.6% to foreign currency. Gross profit rose 2% to $370 million, but gross margin fell to 32% of sales from 35% a year earlier as cost of products and services sold climbed 16% on volume and raw-material inflation in RAS. The cost of independence shows below the line: SG&A rose 17% to $123 million on headcount added to run a standalone public company, and interest and other financial charges jumped to $23 million from $2 million after the debt issued around the spin-off. Income before taxes fell 12% to $176 million. Net income attributable to Solstice still rose 23% to $119 million, helped by a lower 23.7% effective tax rate against 50.5% a year earlier, when nondeductible transaction costs inflated the prior-year rate. Note that $15 million of the $134 million total net income accrued to noncontrolling interests, a much larger deduction than a year earlier, so the headline growth overstates the shareholder gain. Reported diluted EPS was $0.75 and adjusted diluted EPS $0.88. On a full-year basis, FY25 revenue was $3.9B (+3.1%) with net income of $237M and diluted EPS of $1.49, down from $3.74 in FY24; the FY23–FY25 diluted EPS series of $3.91, $3.74 and $1.49 reflects the spin and interest step-down rather than an operating collapse.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The spin transformed the balance sheet. Total equity fell from $3.2B at FY24 to $1.4B at FY25, and total debt went from $0.0B to $2.0B over the same span, swinging net debt from -$0.7B (a net cash position) to $1.4B. Cash and short-term investments ended FY25 at $0.5B, down from $0.7B. The current ratio eased to 1.39 at FY25 from 1.72 a year earlier and stood at 1.46 on a trailing-twelve-month basis. Management frames the leverage as manageable: at June 30, 2026 it reported total long-term debt of $2.0 billion, cash and cash equivalents of approximately $750 million, a net leverage ratio of approximately 1.3x on trailing adjusted EBITDA, and total liquidity of approximately $1.75 billion including $1.0 billion of revolver availability. That cushion matters because the pending Element Solutions acquisition is supported by an initial $4.685 billion bridge commitment from Goldman Sachs that the company intends to replace with a term loan B and unsecured notes before closing. No EBITDA-based leverage or interest-coverage figure is available from the vendor's structured data, so those ratios are shown as not available and the net-leverage read rests on the company's own adjusted-EBITDA disclosure.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow has stepped down as the business absorbed separation costs, from $0.8B in both FY23 and FY24 to $0.5B in FY25. Capital expenditure held near $0.3B a year across FY23–FY25, so free cash flow fell to $0.1B in FY25 from the half-billion-dollar level of the two prior years, cutting the FCF margin from 14.5% in FY24 to 3.1%. The dominant FY25 cash item was $1.5B of dividends paid, which drove the equity and net-debt swings noted above and reflects distributions made around the separation rather than an ongoing payout of that size. The trailing FCF yield is 2.1%. First-half 2026 signals improvement: the company reported operating cash flow of $461 million and free cash flow of $248 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, with capital expenditures of $186 million, up 35% year over year on planned growth spending. The regular dividend is modest — $0.075 per share declared on July 17, 2026, a 0.51% yield — leaving most cash flow available for debt reduction and the Element Solutions transaction.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing GAAP figures Solstice looks expensive: 43.9x trailing-twelve-month earnings and 2.2x sales, with EV/EBITDA not available from the vendor because no clean EBITDA line is provided. That trailing-twelve-month multiple is elevated because the earnings window now carries the post-spin interest and separation costs that also held FY25 GAAP EPS to $1.49; it is not a claim on the shares' earning power once those costs roll off. Forward multiples tell a different story: the shares trade at 20.1x NTM consensus earnings and about 17.2x FY27E EPS of $3.37, and consensus FY26E EPS of $2.88 sits inside the company's own raised adjusted-EPS guidance of $2.75–$2.95. Q2'26 adjusted diluted EPS was $0.88 against $0.75 reported, illustrating the gap between GAAP and the numbers the Street capitalizes. At the current $57.98, those forward multiples are undemanding for a business that reported a 25.3% adjusted EBITDA margin in Q2'26 and raised its full-year guide to $1,035–$1,055 million of adjusted EBITDA, alongside double-digit organic growth — which is what underpins the Street's Strong Buy stance and $80.25 consensus target. The valuation risk is that GAAP earnings, not adjusted, are what ultimately service the added debt.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Organic growth stays in the double digits, the Element Solutions deal closes in the first half of 2027 and integrates without straining the balance sheet, and the multiple re-rates toward the Street's high-$80s targets as adjusted EBITDA approaches the raised $1,035–$1,055 million guide. Implies a move back toward the 52-week high of $90.80.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Volume-led growth of roughly the 7.0% seen in Q2'26 continues and 2026 lands within the raised $4,125–$4,185 million sales guide, but leverage and deal uncertainty cap the re-rating. The shares close part of the gap to the $80.25 consensus target rather than all of it.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A cyclical slowdown in refrigerants, or a delayed or more dilutive Element Solutions financing, pressures both margins and the multiple; RAS adjusted EBITDA margin, already down 648 basis points year over year to 32.9%, stays soft. The shares fall back toward the lower end of the 52-week range that starts at $40.43.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: The three scenarios weight to a fair value modestly above today's price and produce a reward-to-risk that clears our BUY threshold without reaching STRONG BUY. The Bull case at $88 (30% probability) assumes the growth acceleration holds and the Element Solutions deal is digested cleanly; the Base case at $72 (45%) assumes solid volume-led growth but a capped multiple while leverage and deal risk are resolved; the Bear case at $45 (25%) reflects a cyclical or financing setback and sits more than 15% below the current price, as a real downside case should. The probability-weighted fair value lands inside our $68–$84 target range, whose low end stands above the current $57.98 so the upside line reads positive. The dominant source of dispersion is the Element Solutions transaction: its timing, final financing mix and integration will do more to determine which scenario plays out than any single quarter of organic results.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Solstice reports a single consolidated result in the vendor's FY25 data, with revenue of $3.9B, though it manages the business through two operating segments that it breaks out in its Q2'26 release. Refrigerants & Applied Solutions (RAS), the larger of the two, posted Q2'26 net sales of $850 million, up 12% year over year, spanning low global warming potential refrigerants, blowing agents, aerosols and nuclear-conversion services under the Solstice, Genetron and Aclar brands. Electronic & Specialty Materials (ESM) posted $298 million, up 8%, covering electronic materials, high-strength fibers and life-science chemicals under the Spectra, Fluka and Hydranal brands. Consolidated Q2'26 net sales rose 11% to $1,148 million, driven mainly by volume. The mix skews toward regulated, qualification-heavy end markets — HVAC/R, nuclear energy, semiconductors, defense and healthcare — where positions are sticky but exposed to raw-material inflation and cyclicality.

moatFactors.name: Regulatory-driven refrigerant transition
moatFactors.body: Solstice's low global warming potential refrigerants sell into a market shaped by environmental regulation that favors LGWP chemistry, and Refrigerants net sales rose 13% to $473 million in Q2'26. Regulation cuts both ways — the same 10-K risk factors flag that changing rules could require costly product changes — so the tailwind is real but not guaranteed.

moatFactors.name: Intellectual property and brands
moatFactors.body: The company holds over 5,700 patents and pending applications and sells through long-established brands — Solstice, Genetron, Aclar, Spectra, Fluka and Hydranal — that carry qualification and switching costs in regulated end markets such as healthcare packaging and life-science reagents.

moatFactors.name: Specialized, qualified positions
moatFactors.body: In nuclear conversion services and semiconductor materials, products must be qualified into customer processes, which slows share loss; Nuclear rose 27% and Electronic Materials rose 15% in Q2'26, faster than the group. Solstice serves over 3,000 customers across approximately 120 countries from 20 manufacturing sites.

moatFactors.name: Cost position and cyclicality
moatFactors.body: The moat does not extend to pricing power over inputs: cost of products and services sold rose 16% in Q2'26 on raw-material inflation, group gross margin has fallen from 35.2% in FY23 to 32.2% in FY25, and the business is exposed to seasonal and cyclical demand per its own risk factors.

businessMoat.durability: The competitive position is durable in pockets but not company-wide, which supports a narrow rather than wide moat. Qualified positions in nuclear conversion, semiconductor materials, healthcare packaging and specialty fibers are sticky, and regulation that favors low global warming potential chemistry gives RAS a structural tailwind. Against that, the 10-K lists intense competition, raw-material inflation, and seasonal and cyclical demand as material risks, and group gross margin has already compressed over FY23 to FY25 as noted above. The bigger swing to durability is external: the pending Element Solutions acquisition would enlarge the specialty-materials platform but also test whether Solstice can integrate and de-lever, and until it closes the standalone track record remains short.

points: Sales growth has accelerated from low single digits under Honeywell (FY24 +3.3%, FY25 +3.1%) to 11% in Q2'26, with volume (7.0%) contributing more than price (3.6%).
Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to net sales of $4,125–$4,185 million and adjusted diluted EPS of $2.75–$2.95, and guided third-quarter net sales to $990–$1,030 million.
Consensus sees revenue rising from FY25's $3.9B to $4.2B in FY26E and $4.4B in FY27E, with EPS climbing from $2.88 to $3.37 as spin costs roll off.

Growth was broad across both segments in Q2'26: Nuclear (+27%) and Healthcare Packaging (+24%) led the higher-margin RAS segment, while Electronic Materials rose 15% on semiconductor-driven volume within ESM, whose 21.6% adjusted EBITDA margin sits below the group.
The pending Element Solutions acquisition, expected to close in the first half of 2027, is the step-change growth lever — and the primary execution risk — layered on top of the organic base.

management.leadership: Solstice is led by David Sewell, President and Chief Executive Officer, with Tina Pierce as Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. The two operating segments are run by named executives — Jeffrey Dormo leads Refrigerants and Applied Solutions and Simon Mawson leads Electronic and Specialty Materials — and Jason Clifford serves as Chief Human Resources Officer. The team is executing its first full year as a standalone public company after the October 30, 2025 spin-off, and the Q2'26 result of 11% net-sales growth with raised full-year guidance is early evidence that the standalone operation is functioning. The most consequential decision on the table is the proposed acquisition of Element Solutions, which Sewell frames as accelerating the build of a scaled advanced-materials platform aligned with AI, data centers, nuclear energy and semiconductor manufacturing.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is dominated by the balance-sheet reset from the spin and the pending deal. FY25 included $1.5B of dividends paid — distributions tied to the separation, not a recurring payout — alongside the assumption of about $2.0B of total debt. Since separating, the company has set a modest regular dividend of $0.075 per share (a 0.51% yield) and is directing free cash flow toward the balance sheet, reporting a net leverage ratio of approximately 1.3x and total liquidity of approximately $1.75 billion at June 30, 2026. Capital expenditure is being stepped up deliberately — $186 million in the first half of 2026, up 35% year over year, with full-year capex guided to $420–$440 million — to support growth. The defining choice is the Element Solutions acquisition: a cash-and-stock deal whose bridge financing, described in the balance-sheet discussion above, management intends to term out into permanent debt before closing, which will set the leverage profile for years.
management.governance: Governance rests on the April 2, 2026 DEF 14A proxy statement in the pack. The board's Corporate Governance Guidelines call for a substantial majority of independent directors, and the board affirmatively determined that nine non-employee directors — Gautam, Gibbons, Oplinger, Somasundaram, Trerotola, Ward, Worrell, Laird and Lee — meet Nasdaq and SEC independence standards; only CEO David Sewell is not independent. The proxy states that no non-employee director receives direct compensation from Solstice other than under the director program, has an immediate family member paid by the company outside non-executive employment, or is affiliated with Solstice or its subsidiaries. Audit and Compensation Committee members meet the additional Nasdaq independence requirements. Executive pay is described as emphasizing variable, at-risk compensation linked to performance, appropriate for a newly public company still building its track record.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider ownership is minimal, as is typical for a company less than a year removed from a spin-off. As of the March 23, 2026 record date, all directors, nominees and executive officers as a group (15 people) beneficially owned 115,321 shares — 16,404 held outright plus 98,917 they have the right to acquire — which the proxy notes is less than 1% of shares outstanding. Among individuals, CFO Tina Pierce held 37,832 total shares (including 29,141 options), more than any other named officer or director, while CEO David Sewell's line in the ownership table shows no beneficially owned shares. Non-employee directors each held small positions built largely from 1,786 unvested RSUs. Insider alignment is therefore still forming, and equity stakes should build as post-spin grants vest.

idiosyncratic: Element Solutions execution and financing. The cash-and-stock acquisition ($10.00 plus 0.500 Solstice shares per Element share) depends on terming out the bridge financing noted above into permanent debt before an expected first-half-2027 close; adverse credit markets, a failed vote or a botched integration would each hit the equity. Termination fees are asymmetric and material — Solstice could owe Element $385.0 million or $513 million under certain circumstances, versus $376.0 million the other way.

Leverage layered on a young balance sheet. The spin took total debt from $0.0B to $2.0B and equity from $3.2B to $1.4B in a single year; interest and other financial charges jumped to $23 million in Q2'26 from $2 million a year earlier, and no EBITDA-based coverage ratio is available to size the cushion independently.

Margin and cyclicality. RAS adjusted EBITDA margin fell 648 basis points to 32.9% in Q2'26, group gross margin has slid from 35.2% in FY23 to 32.2% in FY25, and the 10-K flags seasonal and cyclical demand plus raw-material inflation as material risks; refrigerants and HVAC/R demand can turn with the economy.

Limited standalone history and Honeywell overhang. Solstice has less than a year of independent results, its own risk factors warn the Honeywell-era financials may not predict future results, and Tax Matters Agreement provisions with Honeywell could constrain the Element Solutions deal or trigger indemnities.

GAAP versus adjusted gap. The equity case leans on adjusted metrics — Q2'26 adjusted diluted EPS of $0.88 against $0.75 reported — and if one-time costs prove more persistent than guided, the 43.9x trailing GAAP multiple is a reminder of how thin reported earnings currently are.
risks.systemic: Solstice is exposed to the broad macro and policy backdrop its MD&A describes as volatile: geopolitical conflict, foreign-currency swings, and energy and commodity price fluctuations that raise input costs and disrupt supply chains. Tariffs and evolving trade policy are a specific channel, and the company says it relies on supply-chain simplification, dual sourcing and pricing actions to mitigate them. As a chemicals manufacturer it also carries systemic environmental, safety and regulatory exposure — climate-related regulation, negative perceptions of nuclear energy, and the inherent hazards of chemical production are all cited in the 10-K. Finally, as a recently listed company, the stock is sensitive to credit conditions and equity-market sentiment, which matters more than usual while a large debt-financed acquisition is pending. A 52-week range of $40.43 to $90.80 shows how wide the market's own view has already swung.

body: Our call is BUY, with a target range of $68 to $84. At $57.98 the shares discount much of the transition risk from the Honeywell spin while giving limited credit for the growth acceleration now visible in the numbers: Q2'26 net sales up 11% to $1,148 million, full-year 2026 guidance raised to $4,125–$4,185 million of sales and $2.75–$2.95 of adjusted EPS, and forward multiples of 20.1x NTM and about 17.2x FY27E that sit well below the Street's $80.25 consensus target.

The BUY is conditional, not unqualified. It rests on organic momentum holding and on the Element Solutions acquisition closing without straining a balance sheet that already carries about $2.0B of debt and a $4.685 billion bridge behind the deal. The bear case at $45 — more than 15% below today's price — is a genuine outcome if leverage, integration or refrigerant cyclicality goes the wrong way, and reported GAAP earnings remain thin at a 43.9x trailing multiple.

Watch three things into 2027: the pace of organic growth against the $990–$1,030 million third-quarter guide, the final financing mix and timing of the Element Solutions deal expected to close in the first half of 2027, and whether RAS margins recover toward the mid-30% level management expects in the second half of 2026. Progress on all three would move the stock toward the upper half of our range; a stumble on any would validate the bear case.
